newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. planes, carrier head for Gulf in Iraq crisis.
newsitem.headline: U.S. planes, carrier head for Gulf in Iraq crisis.

text.p: U.S. fighter planes and an aircraft carrier headed to the Gulf on Friday for widely expected attacks to punish Iraqi President Saddam Hussein for defying Western patrols of no-fly zones over Iraq.

But the eight advanced F-117A stealth fighters, the same kind used in the 1991 Gulf War to evade Iraqi air defences and pound targets in the centre of Baghdad, were not due to arrive in Kuwait until late on Friday. It appeared unlikely that U.S. forces would strike before Saturday at the earliest.

The aircraft carrier Enterprise, with 75 warplanes, was expected to steam from the Adriatic Sea through the Suez Canal by the weekend to join the carrier Carl Vinson. The two ships have F-14 fighters adapted to carry accurate laser-guided bombs.

The U.S. Army said it was sending two Patriot anti-missile batteries, used as a defence against Iraqi Scud missiles during the Gulf War, to the Gulf in coming days. U.S. B-52 bombers are already at a British base on the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia within striking distance of Iraq.

The time needed to put extra U.S. forces in place, and some softening in the rhetoric from Washington, appeared to open at least a small window of opportunity for diplomatic efforts to ease the latest crisis between the United States and Iraq.
Turkey's ambassador in Washington on Thursday sounded a warning against further military strikes and called for a diplomatic-oriented strategy towards Baghdad.
The ambassador, Nuzhet Kandemir, also said that Ankara was providing aircraft to help the United States fly 2,500 Americans, Kurds and Iraqi dissidents out of northern Iraq.

Last week U.S. planes and ships fired 44 cruise missiles at southern Iraqi air defences in retaliation for an Iraqi military action against a Kurdish faction in the north. Iraqi troops on August 31 intervened on the side of one Kurdish group to help it wrest control of a key city from rival guerrillas.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, campaigning for re-election, faced renewed criticism from Republican Party opponents and analysts who questioned the wisdom of the military confrontation with Saddam, a survivor of the Gulf War and more than six years of U.N. sanctions imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
Led by vice-presidential contender Jack Kemp, Republicans complained that Clinton had not been firm enough in dealing with Iraq and demanded closer consultations before any attack.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said U.S. forces had "robust rules of engagement" when provoked but did not repeat an earlier warning that the response would be "disproportionate".

Former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker, who helped organise the coalition that drove Iraqi forces out of Kuwait in the Gulf War, said the United States should "at least consider military targets in and around Baghdad and Republican Guard units north of the 36th parallel".
"I think they really only understand disproportionate force," he told the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Clinton himself said on Thursday: "I don't want to get in a word war with Saddam Hussein, but we're going to do whatever it takes to keep him from threatening his neighbours, threatening our pilots, and we're going to enforce the no-fly zone."

The latest U.S. moves came after Iraq fired a missile at two U.S. fighters patrolling the no-fly zone over northern Iraq on Wednesday. The Pentagon said Iraq fired three missiles over southern Iraq on Thursday but they came nowhere near U.S. and allied planes.
U.S. officials said they detected no movement of Iraqi forces south toward Kuwait.
Rising tensions have pushed oil prices up to levels unseen since January 1991, the eve of the Gulf War.
But the allied unity displayed then has been notably lacking in the latest crisis, and Baghdad has revelled in the disarray.

As the U.S. military buildup went into high gear, France said it was deeply concerned about rising tensions in the Gulf and Russia said the use of force in Iraq without approval of the U.N. Security Council was unacceptable.
The Security Council on Thursday said it was still behind the oil-for-food deal for Iraq that has been on hold since Baghdad sent troops into northern Iraq.

But the Council was too divided on the latest crisis to issue a formal statement telling Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to implement the oil-for-food plan as soon as possible, as Italy had proposed.
